Pre-existing and independent of the ADL free-callee fix: the definitions and the `using` line are rendered from the source name either way, and the pre-fix call sites spelled the same mangled names unqualified. Fix shape: make the definition/declaration name and the re-export read the SAME `literal_mangled_name` decision the call site reads -- one naming fact per overload variant, consulted by every emitter, rather than a rename applied only on the stub/impl path. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (rejects valid, wrong site / misleading) A name the implicit `tpy` package does not export is accepted at the `from tpy import` line and only fails at the first USE, as `Unknown type: X`.** [`tpy-import-unknown-name-undiagnosed`] `/tmp/agents/probe_Int32/main.py` -- `from tpy import Int32` then `x: Int32 = 5` -- takes the import silently and reports `main.py:4: error: Unknown type: Int32` (verified 2026-09-14 on 0.6.0.dev0, clean export). Every other module diagnoses the import itself: the same shape over a user module (`/tmp/agents/probe_unknown_import/`, `from mod import Nope`) gives `main.py: error: 'Nope' not found in module 'mod'` (raised at `tpyc/sema/analyzer.py:3890`), and `from tpy import ...` should say the same. Two faces:
  - **(a) no import-site check.** The parser's dedicated `tpy` branch (`tpyc/parse/imports.py:463-473`) adds every `(original_name, local_name)` pair to `imports["tpy"]` unconditionally, without consulting `get_tpy_exports()` (`tpyc/parse/imports.py:165`) -- the export set it already resolves one branch earlier for `from tpy import *`. Sema's import pass then routes the name through the `elif import_module_name == "tpy":` arm (`tpyc/sema/analyzer.py:581-590`) instead of `_register_user_module_import`, and both helpers that arm calls are silent no-ops for a name the module does not define: `_register_tpy_type_alias` (`:3511`) returns when the alias table has no entry, `_register_implicit_module_variable` (`:3475`) returns `False` when `module_info.variables` has none. So the one site that raises `'X' not found in module 'Y'` is never reached for `tpy`. The check belongs at one of those two sites, over the same export set.
  - **(b) no hint for the pre-rename scalar spellings.** `Int32` / `UInt8` / `Float64` / ... are the pre-2026-09-12 spellings of the scalar types, renamed to lowercase (`int32`, `uint8`, `float64`, ...). `grep -rn '\bInt32\b\|\bUInt8\b\|\bFloat64\b\|\bInt64\b' lib/` matches nothing: `lib/tpy/tpy/__init__.py` exports only the lowercase names (`__all__` lines 55-56: `"int8", "int16", "int32", "int64",` / `"uint8", ...`) and the CPython stubs define only those too (`lib/cpy/tpy/__init__.py:138`: `int32 = _make_fixed_int_type("int32", 32, True)`). Both sites -- the import-site error from (a) and the use-site `Unknown type:` (`tpyc/parse/type_resolver.py:530`) -- should carry a *did you mean `int32`?* hint when the unknown name case-folds onto a known scalar, which is the whole old-spelling set since the rename was mechanical.

- **[LOW small] (cpy-phase parity gap) The CPython `float32` stub rounds a `float`-typed VARIABLE operand to single precision, where TPy widens to double.** [`cpy-float32-double-precision`] `lib/cpy/tpy/__init__.py`'s `float32` class rounds every operand and result through `struct.pack('f', ...)`, which matches TPy for float32, int and float-LITERAL operands (a literal takes float32 in TPy). A `float`-typed variable operand (`f32 + d` with `d: float`) is a double in TPy (`__add__(self, other: float) -> float`) but a float32 under the stub, since Python cannot tell a literal from a variable at runtime. A case that prints such a mixed result cannot run under the cpy phase. Narrowed 2026-09-12 from the previous alias-of-float gap.

- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, loud) Slice assignment on a user record with a slice-keyed `__setitem__` is rejected outright.** [`record-slice-assign-rejected`]
  `g[0:2] = 9` on a record whose `__setitem__` takes `slice` fails at sema with `Slice assignment not supported for type 'Own[Grid]'`, while the plain `g[0] = 5` resolves and CPython runs both. The rule predates the dunder lookup; a slice key should resolve through `__setitem__` like any other. Found while closing the `@dispatch` `__getitem__` operator gap (2026-09-10).
- **[MED small] (unlocated diagnostic; ill-formed C++ inside a tuple) A `bytes` value at a `bytearray` PARAMETER never reaches the located cross-buffer rule.** [`bytes-at-bytearray-param-unlocated`] `def f(b: bytearray)` called as `f(p)` with `p: bytes` rejects at `call.arg_shape.record_nonf1`, and the tuple form `def f(t: tuple[bytearray, int])` called as `f((p, 1))` is accepted by sema outright and fails in the C++ toolchain -- codegen emits `std::tuple<ByteArray*, ...>{&(p), ...}`, taking the address of a `bytes` value for a `ByteArray*` slot. A `bytearray` is a reference type, so its parameter takes the reference/pointer form and the argument never routes through the value-bind check the rule lives on; the OWNING sinks of the same direction (a local, a field, a return) do reach it and give the `write 'bytearray(...)' around it` message. Pre-existing and unchanged by the tuple-element fix (verified against a detached worktree at 578932992e: identical on both). The fix is to route the reference-typed parameter bind through the same check, not to add a second one. Met 2026-09-10 while sweeping the recursive arms of `_check_compat`. The opposite direction -- a `bytearray` at a `bytes` parameter -- has the same gap and is silent rather than loud: [`bytearray-at-bytes-param-owned-silently`].

- **[MED small] (ill-formed C++, toolchain-caught) Binding the result of `dict.setdefault` on an `R | None` element type fails the C++ build.** [`dict-setdefault-optional-elem-result-ill-formed`] `d: dict[str, Pic | None] = {}; got = d.setdefault("a", Pic(3))` (or `None`, or a pointer-repr Optional local) renders `Pic* got = ::tpy::dict_setdefault(d, "a", ...)`, binding the returned `std::optional<Pic>&` to a `Pic*` -- the result gate admits the call but the Optional-element read-back has no lift (the sibling of the entry below); the call as a STATEMENT lowers. Found 2026-09-11 while admitting the pointer-repr Optional local at the argument slot; the argument was never what failed. Pre-existing on master `331fbc2948`.
- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) Reading an `Optional` element back out of a container does not lower.** [`optional-container-element-read-unlowered`] With `d: dict[str, bytes | None] = {"k": b"ab"}`, `v = d["k"]` rejects at `stmt.var_decl:subscript.elem.optional` and `for v in d.values()` at `stmt.for_each:iter.method_call_shape`, while the STORE and `len(d)` both lower; CPython reads it back with no ceremony. The `list[bytes | None]` sibling rejects at the same tag; a for-each over a reference-typed `list[R | None]` (`for p in patches:`) rejects at `stmt.for_each:foreach.consuming_iter` while the index read `p = patches[i]` lowers. It is otherwise the VALUE-typed payload that fails, not Optional elements in general: the reference-typed `dict[str, R | None]` reads back and runs. Pre-existing and unrelated to the cross-buffer rule (no bytearray is involved in any witness); met 2026-09-10 while pinning that rule's wrapped face, which is why `tests/cases/bytes/bytearray_copy_into_bytes_sink` observes its copy on an Optional LOCAL and only counts the dict one.

- **[LOW small] (message quality; the rejection itself is correct) The container-LITERAL element seam rewrites every targeted diagnostic raised under it, so the remediation is lost.** [`literal-elem-seam-swallows-remediation`] `_analyze_list_literal`'s contextual arm wraps its per-element `check_type_compatible` in `except SemanticError` and re-raises a fixed *List literal element N has type X, incompatible with annotated element type Y*. Any rule that fires INSIDE that call and carries a fix -- the mismatch's conversion hint *write 'bytes(...)' around it*, `_check_polymorphic_slicing`'s *use `Box[Throwable]`* -- is replaced by the generic text, so the user is told what is wrong but not what to write. The dict/set literal arms wrap the same way. Pre-existing (the slicing hint has been swallowed there since it was added); surfaced 2026-09-10 when the bytearray-at-an-owning-bytes-sink rule reached the literal face. The fix needs a way for a targeted diagnostic to survive the wrapper (a marker on `SemanticError`, or the seam asking `_check_compat` first and framing only its `CompatError`) -- a shared-diagnostic change, so it is filed rather than improvised. `tests/cases/bytes/error_bytearray_in_bytes_literal` pins the seam's text as it stands. The same wrap-and-swallow shape recurs at the LAMBDA-RETURN check (`tpyc/sema/expressions.py` ~4180-4188), so a general fix should cover both rather than unwrapping the literal arm alone. A third face is the CONTAINER-INVARIANT path (`tpyc/sema/compatibility.py` ~1199/1354/1375), which does not wrap a raised diagnostic but builds its own `CompatError` from the element pair and so never reaches the hint: `d2: dict[int, bytes] = d1` over a `dict[int, bytearray]` reports *expected bytes, got bytearray* and the `list` twin *expected list[bytes], got list[bytearray]*, both correct rejections with no *write 'bytes(...)' around it*. Verified identical at 305c187198, before the hint became data, so it is pre-existing there too; the fix shape is the same -- let the element check's own error through instead of re-forming one. A fourth face: an owning UNION-typed sink (`bytes | Indexed` field written from a bytearray) rejects through `_check_compat`'s union member loop, which asks the row veto per member but computes the *write 'bytes(...)' around it* hint only for the direct pair, so the message arrives without it. Same fix shape.

- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) An `Own[bytes]` parameter takes only a bytes LITERAL: every other source rejects.** [`own-bytes-param-takes-only-a-literal`] With `def take(b: Own[bytes]) -> int`, `take(b"ab")` lowers while `take(bytes(x))` (a call rvalue), `take(name)` (an owned `bytes` local) and the `BytesView`-typed local all reject at `call.arg_shape.own_bytes`; the constructor twin `H(bytes(x))` / `H(name)` rejects at `call.ctor_arg.own_bytes` while `H(b"ab")` lowers. The `Own[bytes]` CONTAINER-ELEMENT slot (`xs.append(bytes(x))`) takes all of them, so the gap is the non-element `Own[bytes]` slot rather than the payload: `_bytes_owned_slot_arg` / `_bytes_owned_name_arg` / `_bytes_owned_call_rvalue_arg` in `tpyc/thir/lower/checks.py` are reached from the element seam only. Pre-existing (no bytearray is involved in any witness). Found while pinning the bytearray-at-an-owning-bytes-sink rule; `tests/cases/bytes/bytearray_copy_into_bytes_sink` covers the element face and says why the other two are absent.


- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A generic record that INHERITS its `__init__` cannot be constructed at a view-family instantiation.** [`inherited-generic-ctor-view-arg`] `class Derived[T](Base[T]): pass` over `class Base[T]` with `def __init__(self, value: T)` rejects `Derived[str]("hi")` at `expr.call:call.ctor_arg.generic`, while `Base[str]("hi")` lowers through the same argument and `Derived[int32](5)` lowers through the same route -- so it is the pair (inherited `__init__`, view-family instantiation), not either alone. Reproducer `/tmp/agents/stringtype_impl/probe_move/derived.py`. Found by the merge hunt 2026-09-09. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (uncompilable C++, toolchain-caught) Indexing a string LITERAL directly is ambiguous in C++.** [`str-literal-index-ambiguous`] `print("xyz"[1])` renders `::tpy::__getitem__("xyz", 1)` with a `const char[4]` argument, and `dunder.hpp` offers `__getitem__(const std::string&, int32_t)` and `__getitem__(std::string_view, int32_t)` -- two user-defined conversions of equal rank, so g++ reports *call of overloaded '__getitem__(const char [4], int)' is ambiguous*. Binding the literal to a local first (`s = "xyz"; s[1]`) compiles and runs, and the SLICE form (`"abc"[0:2]`) compiles because `str_slice` takes the view alone, so it is the index form on a bare literal only. `__len__` already carries a `const char*` overload for exactly this reason; the fix is the same one line for `__getitem__`. Pre-existing and identical on master (probed at 561766ec7e in a detached worktree). No case in the corpus indexes a bare literal. Found probing subscripts after the dispatch-split merge 2026-09-10.


- **[MED small] (hard C++ error) An escaping nested `def` emits a by-value capture with no copyability check.** [`nesteddef-copy-capture-uncheckable`] Sema's "used after the closure -- must copy, warn" branch (`tpyc/sema/analyzer.py`, the `should_move` / `names_used_after` split) leaves the name out of `move_captures`, and the nested-`def` capture-list builder (`tpyc/thir/lower/statements.py`, the `stmt.escapes` arm) then spells it bare. Nothing asks whether C++ can copy it, so a record with `__del__` (or a `@nocopy` field) is emitted as `[g]` and g++ rejects the generated file: `g = Guard(5)` + an escaping `def inner(): return g.x` + a later `print(g.x)` warns "Escaping closure 'inner' copies local 'g' ..." and then fails with `use of deleted function 'Guard::Guard(const Guard&)'` (reproducer `/tmp/agents/gatefix/d/nested2.py`). The LAMBDA sibling of the same shape rejects in the front end (`expr.lambda`, via `_uncopyable_capture`), so the two closure forms disagree on the same capture. Fix shape: ask `_cpp_noncopyable_type` at the nested-`def` by-value entry the way the lambda entry builder does, and decide whether the answer is a front-end reject or an upgrade of the copy WARNING to an error -- the warning is already at the right site, it just does not know the copy is impossible. **Dormant sibling in the same predicate:** `_cpp_noncopyable_type` does not recurse into `TupleType` elements, so a value tuple whose element is a ValueType with `__del__` reads as copyable; `_uncopyable_capture` now walks the element tree itself (`TupleType.has_nested_element`), but every other caller of the predicate still does not. Unreachable end-to-end today (`t[0]` on such a tuple hits the unrelated `subscript.tuple_shape` reject), so no case pins it. Found fixing the borrowed-param capture peel.

- **[MED small] (silent CPython divergence) Re-packing the elements of an OWNING tuple frame local into a fresh tuple yield copies the reference element with no warning.** [`tuple-repack-yield-silent-elem-copy`] `t = (i, C(i * 10))` in a generator declared `Iterator[tuple[int32, Own[C]]]`, then `yield (t[0], t[1])`, emits `return std::tuple<int32_t, C>{std::get<0>((*t)), std::get<1>((*t))};` -- `std::get<1>((*t))` copy-constructs the `C` out of the frame slot. The consumer's `pair[1].v = 777` is then invisible to the generator's own `t[1].v` read after the resume: TPy prints `gen sees 0` / `gen sees 10` where CPython prints `gen sees 777` twice (probe `/tmp/agents/probe15/pF.py`). The WHOLE-slot form at the same site (`yield t`) does warn ("copies tuple[int32, C] into owned storage; use copy() to make this explicit"), so the element-wise re-pack loses a diagnostic the enclosing shape has. `docs/PITFALLS.md#silent-copy-vs-alias` + `#copy-warning-at-wrong-site`. Pre-existing and identical on both the simple-generator peephole and the resumable frame -- unaffected by the frame's tuple-yield name arms, which cover the whole-slot source only. Fix shape: reach the per-element copy diagnostic (`warn_tuple_literal_member_copy`) from a tuple LITERAL whose members are subscripts of an owning tuple binding, the way the whole-name source reaches `warn_pointer_repr_tuple_copy`. Found analysing the tuple-yield ladders for the peephole deletion. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (warned, not silent) The tuple-copy warning at a yield names the copy but not its aliasing consequence.** [`tuple-yield-copy-warning-omits-aliasing`] A generator whose owning tuple local is still live after the yield copies the tuple out (`return (*t);`), so the consumer gets its own `C` and a mutation through the yielded element never reaches the generator: TPy `gen sees 0` / `gen sees 10` where CPython prints `gen sees 777` twice (probe `/tmp/agents/probe15/pB.py`). The divergence IS declared -- sema emits "copies tuple[int32, C] into owned storage; use copy() to make this explicit" -- but the text describes the cost (a copy) rather than the semantic change (the consumer no longer aliases the generator's object), which is the part a reader has to act on. Same text at every owned-storage sink, so the wording is a shared decision, not a yield-local one. Fix shape: extend the message with the aliasing clause where the source is a reference element the caller can observe through. Found analysing the tuple-yield ladders for the peephole deletion.

- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A generator cannot yield a tuple with a `@nocopy` element, on the premise that `__next__()` hands out a copy -- which the resumable frame does not.** [`nocopy-tuple-yield-gate-stale`] `Iterator[tuple[int32, Own[Handle]]]` at an `@nocopy` `Handle` is rejected at registration: "Generator cannot yield non-copyable type 'tuple[int32, Own[Handle]]': each yielded value is stored by value and handed out as a copy by __next__(), which requires a copy constructor." (probe `/tmp/agents/probe15/pG.py`). The resumable frame's `__next__` returns `std::expected<T, ::tpy::StopIteration>` BY VALUE and the owning frame slot is movable -- a dead-after-yield slot already renders `return std::move((*t));` for the copyable sibling -- so the copy the message asserts is not the one the frame makes. The gate closes the whole `Iterator[tuple[..., Own[@nocopy]]]` family before lowering ever sees it. Fix shape: make the gate ask whether the yield hands out a MOVE at this slot (the same liveness fact the move arm reads) rather than assuming a copy, and keep the reject for the shapes that genuinely copy. Found analysing the tuple-yield ladders for the peephole deletion. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, loud) A tuple literal cannot contain the char produced by string indexing.** [`char-tuple-literal-admission`]
  Inside a narrowed `case str()` arm, `one = (x[0],)` rejects at `decl.tuple_literal_shape`, while the scalar `x[0]` and the byte-valued tuple sibling compile. `_value_tuple_element_ok` in `tpyc/thir/lower/predicates.py` excludes char; the nested value-tuple and tuple-declaration gates inherit that exclusion before lowering the element expression. This predicate and its explicit char exclusion predate the master merge at `987d04c5`. CPython's string-index result is a normal one-character string and can be stored in a tuple. Fix shape: assess char element construction, storage and reads across tuple positions together, preserving the scalar element's value semantics. **Measured 2026-09-15** while fixing the char-at-a-`str`-slot family: this is NOT that family's root -- `(x[0],)` has no `str` slot, its type is `tuple[char]`, so no coercion is involved and the char-to-string conversion those sinks now read does nothing here. Adding `_eligible_char` to `_value_tuple_element_ok` admits the LITERAL and moves the reject one gate on, to the element READ (`one[0]` -> `subscript.tuple_shape`), which is what makes this its own unit: every tuple position (literal, subscript read, param, return, unpack, container element, field) has to be walked, and `_eligible_char`'s own docstring names the reason char was held out of `_eligible_scalar` -- a str literal in a char slot renders a target-typed C++ char literal, which the scalar positions do not thread. Found while adding scalar/tuple controls for narrowed indexing; the passing regression uses the byte-valued sibling. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, loud) A comparison whose operand is a SUBCLASS of the record dunder's declared parameter is rejected.** [`record-eq-subtype-operand-rejects`]
  With `class Puddle(Dog)` and `Dog.__eq__(self, other: "Dog")`, `d == p` rejects at `stmt.expr_stmt:binop.shape.==.record`; CPython runs it (`True` when `Puddle` inherits the dunder, `False` when it overrides it -- Python gives a SUBCLASS operand's method priority in BOTH operand orders). The reject fires whether or not `Puddle` overrides `__eq__`, so it also refuses the shape where the upcast is plainly right. Same row as `BUGS.md#derived-ne-unchecked-operand`: `_record_dunder_operand_pair` (`tpyc/thir/lower/predicates.py`) gates the operand on sema's arg-compatibility predicate, which pins the operand to the declared parameter type rather than admitting a derived one. The explicit `d.__eq__(p)` spelling is accepted (and misbehaves -- see the entry below). **The fix's constraint:** admitting the upcast is only correct when the subclass does NOT override the dunder, or under `@dynamic` dispatch. Records are not polymorphic here, so an admitted upcast static-dispatches to `Dog::__eq__` and silently ignores `Puddle.__eq__` -- which is exactly the divergence the entry below measures at the spellings that already compile. So this reject is the only thing keeping the direct spelling off that divergence: fixing it alone WIDENS the silent one, and the two must land together. Probes `/tmp/agents/puddle/main.py` and `/tmp/agents/refunion_impl/puddle2/main.py`. Found while reviewing the reference-union storage form 2026-09-10. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (SILENT CPython divergence, no warning, two spellings) A record `__eq__` overridden in a subclass is bypassed at every comparison that compiles, and an explicit dunder CALL picks the subclass's where Python does not.** [`record-eq-subclass-static-dispatch`]
  With `Dog.__eq__(self, other: "Dog")` returning `self.n == other.n` and `class Puddle(Dog)` overriding it to `False`, over `d = Dog(1)` and `p = Puddle(1)` (both fields `1`): `d.__eq__(p)` answers **False** where CPython answers True, and `takes(d, p)` / `takes(p, d)` with `def takes(a: Dog, b: Dog): return a == b` answer **True** where CPython answers False. Two different causes, one root -- C++ overload resolution standing in for Python's method lookup: (1) the explicit dunder call renders as the operator (`(d) == (p)`), and C++20's REVERSED candidate makes `Puddle`'s hidden friend `operator==(const Puddle&, const Dog&)` an exact match on both parameters where `Dog`'s needs a derived-to-base conversion, so the subclass's method wins a call that Python defines as unreflected; (2) through base-typed parameters both operands are `const Dog&`, the friends are non-virtual, so `Dog::__eq__` is called and the override is ignored -- Python would give the `Puddle` operand priority. No warning on either. CPython prints `True False` where TPy prints `False True`. Probe `/tmp/agents/refunion_impl/puddle4/main.py` (prints the fields, both explicit-dunder orders and both base-param orders). Sibling of `BUGS.md#record-eq-subtype-operand-rejects`, which is the reject that keeps the DIRECT `d == p` spelling from reaching cause (2); fix shape must decide how a record dunder dispatches when a subclass overrides it (virtual dispatch for an overridden dunder, or a rejection at the spellings that cannot honour Python's rule) rather than widening the operand gate first. Found while reviewing the reference-union storage form 2026-09-10. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A type alias whose body names an IMPORTED type alias is rejected as an unknown type.** [`imported-alias-member-in-alias-body`]
  `from tpy import float64` then `type Mixed = Dog | int32 | float64` fails with `Type alias 'Mixed' references unknown type 'float64'`, and so does the bare `type Alias = float64`. The same type spelled inline in a signature (`def f(x: float64 | str)`) compiles, and a SAME-module alias-of-alias (`type Money = float` then `type A = Money | str`) compiles -- only the imported alias fails. `_validate_type_alias_members` in `tpyc/sema/analyzer.py` accepts a member `NominalType` only when it carries a `_module_qname` or resolves in the record registry; an imported alias binding has neither at that point, so the validator refuses a name it merely has not resolved yet. Reachable from the stdlib today because `float64` is itself an alias (`type float64 = float` in `lib/tpy/tpy/__init__.py`) and from any user module that exports one (`from m import Money`). CPython accepts every spelling. Workaround: spell the underlying type (`float`) or write the union inline -- `tests/cases/union/reference_union_storage_eq` cites this entry and takes the `float` spelling for that reason. Repro `/tmp/agents/refunion_impl/alias5/`. Fix shape: resolve imported alias bindings before the alias-member validation, or let the validator consult the alias table sema already holds -- the same check-runs-before-the-name-is-bound family as the cycle re-export entries. Found spelling the record-beside-numerics pack for the reference-union storage compare 2026-09-10. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, loud) Value-union boundaries reject a bytes member even though its signature and match body can lower.** [`bytes-value-union-boundary-rejects`] When these boundaries widen, the `bytearray_to_bytes` coercion's `identity` disposition (`tpyc/thir/lower/predicates.py`, the `_coerce_disposition` row) has to grow an arm: it assumes the only reachable `bytes` slot is the span view a `bytearray` satisfies bare, but at a union slot the alternative is `const ::tpy::Bytes*`, so an identity pass would render `::tpy::Union<..., const ::tpy::Bytes*>{&ba}` -- ill-formed C++, loud but unlocated. A materialize or a located reject belongs there before the admission widens.
  For `x: bytes | int32`, `if isinstance(x, bytes)` rejects at `stmt.if:cond.call`, before the body reaches subscript lowering. A local `data: bytes | int32 = b"abc"` likewise rejects at `decl.slot_type`. `_eligible_value_union` in `tpyc/thir/lower/predicates.py` admits str/StrView but omits bytes, and `_builtin_value_member` explicitly excludes the BYTES category. The union is value-form, so pointer-union admission cannot rescue it. The isinstance rejection reproduces before the master merge at `987d04c5` and after the match-subscript repair; the local gate uses the same unchanged eligibility predicate. The `bytes | Indexed` pointer-union sibling accepts a bytes-literal call and runs the same indexing body. Fix shape: settle bytes storage/view conversions across value-union construction, arguments, returns and extraction together, rather than widen one consumer. The exact value-union match body remains compile coverage in `tests/cases/match/narrowed_subscript`; its pointer-union sibling supplies native/CPython execution coverage. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, loud) A union with a `BytesView` member does not lower its `isinstance` arm.** [`bytesview-union-member-rejects`] `def f(u: bytes | BytesView)` / `Span[readonly[uint8]] | BytesView` with `if isinstance(u, BytesView):` rejects at `stmt.if:cond.call`, where the same shape over `str | StrView` lowers. The widened union member class (`_ptr_union_member_wide`, `tpyc/thir/lower/predicates.py`) admits `str`, `bytes`, containers, value tuples and `Span` and has no row for the bytes view, so the isinstance narrowing over such a union never reaches the variant machinery. The signature itself renders (`tests/cases/bytes/distinct_spelling_union`, the view pair). Since 2026-09-10 the pair spells distinct alternatives (`::tpy::BytesView` is its own type), so admitting the view is a member-class row, not a spelling question; `tests/cases/bytes/error_bytesview_union_isinstance` pins the reject. Found 2026-09-10 converting the duplicate-spelling error case.

- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) Two union operands of ONE type reject unless they were borrowed the same way.** [`ref-union-loop-var-vs-borrow-compare`]
  A union at a borrow position compares (`union/reference_union_borrow_eq`), but one union type has three C++ renders and none converts to another, so a pair drawn from two of them rejects at `binop.shape.==` although both operands are spelled `Pet` in the source. The three: the STORAGE element a `for e in xs` / comprehension variable binds (`::tpy::Union<Cat, Dog>`), the mutable borrow (`::tpy::Union<Cat*, Dog*>`), and the const-pointee read borrow (`::tpy::Union<const Cat*, const Dog*>`, taken by a `readonly[...]` annotation, by a param the callable only discriminates, and by a local lifted out of a const container). So `[e == u for e in xs]` rejects (at `expr.list_comp`). The two const-side pairs this entry also listed -- `def f(a: readonly[Pet], b: Pet): return a == b` and `def f(xs: list[Pet], u: Pet): a = xs[0]; return a == u` -- now compile: a non-mutating union parameter borrows const pointees, so the annotated and the inferred slot are one render and the const local is that render too. What is left is the STORAGE side. `_ptr_union_compare_pair` (`tpyc/thir/lower/predicates.py`) requires the two renders to agree rather than emit a compare that does not build; before the borrow form was its own type every one of these rejected at the same tag, so nothing regressed -- but CPython runs all three. Fix shape: lift the storage side at the compare, the way an argument at a borrow slot lifts it (`to_const_ptr_variant`) -- a form decision, not a gate widening. `tests/cases/union/reference_union_borrow_eq` cites this entry and takes two parameters in its comprehension section for that reason; its `readonly mixed` and `const local` sections pin the two pairs that now compile. Found landing the borrow-form union type 2026-09-10. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A union whose members are all `Ptr[T]` reaches codegen at one position only.** [`ptr-member-union-unreachable`]
  `type PtrPet = Ptr[Dog] | Ptr[Cat]` renders its alias and a parameter signature (`const ::tpy::Union<Cat*, Dog*>&`) and nothing else: the call that would build the argument rejects at `call.arg_shape.union`, an annotated local at `decl.slot_type`, a return at `return.slot_type`, a field at `ctor.mil_field.union.name`, a container literal at `expr.container_literal`, a compare at `binop.shape.==` (`_eligible_value_union` excludes `Ptr` members, and `_eligible_ptr_union_wide` wants non-value members), and `isinstance(u, Ptr[Dog])` at "Generic type 'Ptr' cannot be used as a value". Identical on `cba2f6df73` and after the borrow-form type landed, so nothing regressed -- but every one of these runs in CPython. **What this entry protects**: such a union is the SAME C++ type as any other union's borrow form -- `::tpy::Union` over a pointer alternative pack -- at every position, owning ones included, because its members are already borrowed references; the consequence is that when it does compare it compares POINTEES, not addresses. It needs no carve-out in the renderer to get there: the alternatives carry the fact. That was decided with the borrow-form type (analysis fork 2.4 answer (i)) and must not be silently re-decided when these gaps close. `tests/cases/union/ptr_member_union_spelling` pins the two spellings that do render. Probes `/tmp/agents/ptrunion/ptrmix/`. Found probing the all-`Ptr` route for the borrow-form union type 2026-09-10. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A `bytearray` member keeps a union element from being read out of a container at all.** [`bytearray-union-element-read-rejects`]
  `a = xs[0]` with `xs: list[bytearray | int32]` rejects at `stmt.var_decl:subscript.elem.union`, with no narrowing or comparison involved; the same read over `list[list[int32] | int32]` or `list[Dog | int32 | float]` lowers and runs. So the union element path is reachable for record, container and scalar members and blocked by the `bytearray` member specifically. CPython runs it. Same `bytearray`-in-a-union family as `BUGS.md#bytes-value-union-boundary-rejects`, and the fix should settle the two together rather than widen one consumer. The third member of the family -- the whole-union deep-const argument bridge, which skipped its wrap because the same narrow member class excluded a zero-type-arg `bytearray` -- is fixed: that consumer now keys on the wide class. Repro `/tmp/agents/ptrunion/cell2.py`. Found spelling the borrowed-value-members section for the borrow-form union compare 2026-09-10. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (ill-formed C++, no diagnostic) Any protocol bound satisfies a `Copyable` requirement, so the bound check accepts a non-copyable type.** [`marker-bound-satisfies-copyable`] `def inner[T: Copyable](v: T)` called from `def outer[T: Stringable](v: T): return inner(v)` is accepted, and so is the end-to-end program that instantiates `outer` at a non-copyable class (a `__del__`, which deletes the generated copy ctor) with `__str__`. `protocols.py` correctly refuses an UNBOUND type param (pinned by `tests/cases/generics/error_copyable_marker_unbound_t`), but when the param HAS a protocol-typed bound the check delegates to that bound, and the `Copyable` marker arm (`tpyc/sema/protocols.py:437`) asks `not is_type_non_copyable(<the protocol type>)` -- False for any protocol, so the negation reports conformance. The bound therefore checks that SOME bound exists, not that it is `Copyable`. Today the owning-slot copy contract (`tpyc/sema/own_copy.py`) still catches the program with a located error, so the consequence is a bound that does not mean what it says rather than a build failure; it becomes a libstdc++-spew class for any future rule that leans on the bound check alone. Fix shape: the marker arm must ask whether the BOUND is (or extends) `Copyable`, not whether the bound type is copyable. Probes `/tmp/agents/bound/p14_any_bound_body.py` and `p15_hole_e2e.py`. Found measuring the explicit-bound fork for the generic copy contract 2026-09-09. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (ill-formed C++, no diagnostic) A generic base in a class header escapes the type-parameter bound check.** [`generic-base-decl-skips-bound-check`] `class Kid(Holder[Pinned])` with `class Holder[T: Copyable]` produces no TPy diagnostic at all; the C++ build then fails with `constraints not satisfied ... concept Copyable = std::is_copy_constructible_v<T>` plus two cascade errors. Every other route to the same instantiation IS checked: explicit type args and constructor inference both report `does not satisfy bound`. Sibling of the unslugged bare-annotation entry further down (`x: Box[Rc[int32]]` is unchecked for the same reason) but a different site: the base list is resolved in `tpyc/sema/registration.py`, which classifies parents without consulting `record_info.type_param_bounds`. Fix shape: validate a parent's substituted type args against the base's bounds where the parents are classified, mirroring the construction-site check. Probe `/tmp/agents/bound/p7_record_base_decl.py`. Found measuring the explicit-bound fork for the generic copy contract 2026-09-09. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (ill-formed C++, no diagnostic) `copy()` of a non-copyable type is not diagnosed, in a generic body or a monomorphic one.** [`copy-call-of-noncopyable-undiagnosed`] `xs.append(copy(v))` with `v: Pinned` (non-copyable: it defines `__del__`) passes sema and fails the C++ build with `use of deleted function 'Pinned::Pinned(const Pinned&)'` at `xs.push_back(::tpyapp::Pinned(v))`; the generic twin `xs.append(copy(v))` at an open `T` instantiated at `Pinned` fails identically at `xs.push_back(T(v))`. Generic and twin agree, and both are wrong. `copy()` is the acknowledged-copy escape hatch and is exempted at record time (`is_copy_call`) before any copy verdict is taken, so nothing downstream asks whether the acknowledged copy is possible. Same class as the `heapq` entry below, whose prescribed fix (add `T: Copyable` bounds) does not cover the monomorphic half. Fix shape: check copy-constructibility at the `copy()` call itself, so the hatch reports what it cannot do. Probes `/tmp/agents/bound/p17_copy_nomove.py` and `p18_copy_nomove_twin.py`. Found measuring the explicit-bound fork for the generic copy contract 2026-09-09. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[HIGH small] (ill-formed C++, toolchain-caught; everyday shape) A local list LITERAL passed to a `readonly[list[T]]` parameter fails the C++ build.** [`array-literal-into-readonly-list-param`] `def f(xs: readonly[list[int32]]) -> int32: ...` called as `bs = [1, 2]; f(bs)`: the literal resolves to `std::array<int32_t, 2>` and the call passes it where the param is `const std::vector<int32_t>&` -> `invalid initialization of reference of type 'const std::vector<int>&' from expression of type 'std::array<int, 2>'`. The same call against a plain `list[int32]` param compiles: passing the local there is what settles the literal as a list. The `readonly[...]` wrapper on the param evidently hides it from that Array-vs-list verdict (not confirmed in code). Records (`[Box(1), Box(2)]`) fail the same way; an annotated local (`bs: list[int32] = [1, 2]`) works. Found 2026-09-20 probing the genexpr entries; no genexpr is involved. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, loud) A tuple with a `StrView` element cannot be built into a list: the literal and `append` forms both reject.** [`strview-tuple-into-list-rejects`] `vs: list[tuple[StrView, int32]] = [(StrView("p"), 1)]` -> `(expr.container_literal)`; `vs.append((StrView("p"), 1))` -> `(expr.tuple_literal)`. READING such a list works, including a genexpr that unpacks it (`sum(len(k) + v for k, v in vs)` compiles since genexprs lower to frames), so the container can be consumed but not produced in TPy. Surfaced 2026-09-20 when the genexpr reject that used to mask it (`genexpr.unpack`) went away; the masking case was `tests/cases/str/error_genexpr_unpack_view_target`.
- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, loud) A walrus target bound inside a generator expression is not visible after it.** [`genexpr-walrus-target-stays-in-frame`] `print(sum(y for x in xs if (y := x * 2) > 2)); print(y)`: CPython binds a comprehension's walrus target in the ENCLOSING function (PEP 572), so the second line prints the last value; TPy analyzes the genexpr body as a generator function of its own, the target becomes a local of that frame, and the later read is `Undefined variable: 'y'`. The genexpr itself computes the right value (`tests/cases/iterators/genexpr_frames`, `walrus`). Never worked: before genexprs were frames the target was bound outward but the lambda did not capture it (a C++ error). Fix shape: a walrus target in a genexpr body is a reference capture of an enclosing local the expression declares, not a frame local. Found 2026-09-20.
- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, located; worked before genexprs were frames) A genexpr capturing a RECORD local that the loop it feeds re-seats is rejected.** [`genexpr-capture-reseated-record`] `n = N(1); for v in (x + n.v for x in xs): out.append(v); n = N(100)` -> `(genexpr.capture_rebound)`. The enclosing body keeps a local that is rebound while something aliases it behind a pointer it re-seats; the frame's capture is a reference to the POINTEE (the body was analyzed against the object), which cannot follow the re-seat, so CPython's late binding (`[2, 102, 103]`) has no sound render and the shape is refused where a rebind can happen between two pulls (`_capture_lvalue`, `tpyc/thir/lower/comprehensions.py`). The closure render captured the pointer variable by reference and followed it. A value-typed or in-place-rebound capture follows the rebind through its reference field, and a record local re-seated OUTSIDE the genexpr's life works (`capture_reseated` in `tests/cases/iterators/genexpr_frames`). Fix shape: a capture param whose enclosing storage is pointer-form is a pointer-form param of the genexpr function (reads spell `->`), bound to the pointer variable itself. Found by the parity review 2026-09-20.
- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, loud) The kept-genexpr rebind scan treats a CONSUMING binding as handing the lazy value on.** [`genexpr-kept-scan-consumer-binding`] `g = relay(x * k for x in xs)` with `k` narrowed, then `total = sum(g)`, then `k = None`, then a read of `total`: rejected with `'k' is narrowed here, but this generator expression is kept past the statement ...`, although `sum(g)` finished the genexpr before the rebind; the same program written `print(sum(g))` compiles. `_names_rebound_while_live` (`tpyc/sema/statements.py`) runs while the BINDING statement is analyzed, so the later statements have no types yet and any statement that reads a kept name and binds another (`h = g`, `total = sum(g)`) extends the kept set; the liveness range then runs to the last read of `total`. The same widening reaches the pointer-kept record capture (`genexpr.capture_rebound`). The error names its escape (bind the narrowed value to a local first). Fix shape: run the check where the kept value's liveness is known with types -- the existing last-use analysis (`ctx.all_last_uses`) owns that fact, and the scan's own line-based range duplicates it and re-walks the body per round. Found by the safety and architecture reviews 2026-09-21.
- **[MED small] (ill-formed C++, toolchain-caught) A generator bound through a tuple-literal unpack copies its frame.** [`generator-bound-by-tuple-unpack`] `g, k = gen(3), 5` then `for v in g:` fails the C++ build with `use of deleted function '__gen_gen::__gen_gen(const __gen_gen&)'`: the desugared halves bind `auto g = __unpack_0_0;`, a COPY of the unpack temp, and a frame is not copyable. `g = gen(3)` alone binds the prvalue. The genexpr form (`g, k = relay(x * k for x in xs), z`) fails the same way, and the kept-genexpr rebind scan does not see `k` rebound there because the rebind and the binding are one statement. Reproduces on master 06dc4b905b with no genexpr. Fix shape: the unpack half moves out of the temp when the element is a frame (or any non-copyable rvalue element). Found by the test-coverage review 2026-09-21.
- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, loud; silent copy before the reject was restored) A genexpr inside a NESTED def that unpacks a record out of tuples of an enclosing container LITERAL is rejected.** [`genexpr-nested-def-literal-record-unpack`] `pairs = [(Node(1), 2), (Node(3), 4)]` then, in a nested def, `sum(p.bump() for p, q in pairs)` -> `(res.local_storage)`. A nested def cannot hand the literal's unsettled Array-vs-list type to ITS enclosing function's finalization, so the genexpr's source goes through the deduced slot, whose native-container adaptor hands back a COPY of each value tuple; aliasing `p` into that copy would lose the mutation silently (TPy `nested 24 4`, CPython `nested 24 24`), so the unpack of a reference member is refused there (`TpyFunction.genexpr_container_by_protocol`). An annotated container (`pairs: list[tuple[Node, int32]] = ...`), the same genexpr outside a nested def, and a plain loop var (no unpack) all alias correctly. A second face of the same limit is a located sema error: a genexpr in a nested def over the enclosing function's literal OF LITERALS (`grid = [[1], [2, 3]]`, then `def inner(): return sum(len(r) for r in grid)`) -> `a generator expression in a nested function cannot iterate a container whose elements are container literals ...; annotate the container where it is created` -- the loop var is a frame field whose container type settles only when the ENCLOSING function ends (pinned by `tests/cases/iterators/error_genexpr_nested_def_literal_elems`; the plain `for r in grid` twin in a nested def rejects at `foreach.elem_family`). Fix shape: let a nested def's pending types ride its enclosing function's finalization, so the source keeps its concrete type. Found by the safety review 2026-09-20.
- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, confusing message) A captured `str | None` or `list[T] | None` narrowed where a genexpr is written, and rebound by the loop the genexpr feeds, fails with a type error about the un-narrowed value.** [`genexpr-unnarrowed-capture-flavors`] `if k is None: return` / `for v in (x + k for x in xs): k = None` at `k: str | None` -> `(binop.shape.+)`; at `k: list[int32] | None` with `len(k)` -> `No matching overload for len(list[int32] | None)`. Where a rebind can happen between two pulls the body is analyzed at the capture's DECLARED type and checks its reads, which works for the flavors that have a checked read (a scalar, a record: warn + runtime check, `narrowed_rebound` in `tests/cases/iterators/genexpr_frames`) and not for these. Sound either way -- nothing compiles that reads a stale narrowing -- but the message does not say what to do (bind the narrowed value to a local first). Found by the safety review 2026-09-20.
- **[MED small] (ill-formed C++, toolchain-caught) A TUPLE-typed loop variable (no unpack) over `enumerate` / `zip` of reference elements fails at the member access: the combinator's tuple member is a REFERENCE where the compiler's tuple borrow form is a POINTER.** [`combinator-tuple-member-ref-vs-pointer-form`] `for p in enumerate(cells): print(p[0], p[1].v)` over `list[Cell]` renders `std::get<1>(p)->v` (`p` is typed as the borrow-form tuple `tuple[int32, Cell]`, whose reference element the compiler spells `Cell*`, see `val_or_ptr_t` in `runtime/cpp/include/tpy/type_traits.hpp` and `tuple_to_storage` in `runtime/cpp/include/tpy/format.hpp`), but `enumerate` yields `std::tuple<int32_t, Cell&>` (`detail::range_member_t`, `runtime/cpp/include/tpy/itertools.hpp`): *base operand of `->` has non-pointer type `Cell`*. A user generator yielding `(i, c)` takes the pointer form (`val_or_ptr_t<T>`) and the same loop compiles; the unpack head (`for i, c in ...`) is unaffected because its per-target bind goes through `tuple_elem_ref`, which normalizes either form. Pre-existing (the member was `val_or_ref_t<T>` = `Cell&` before 2026-09-22 too). Fix shape: ONE tuple borrow form -- the combinators' tuple members spelled `val_or_ptr`-style (`Cell*`, const included) like every other borrow-form tuple, so a tuple-typed consumer needs no second rule; `step_elem_member_t` and the frame unpack targets already deref either. Found 2026-09-22.
- **[MED small] (rejects valid, located) An explicit `readonly[list[T]]` parameter cannot be passed to `enumerate` / `zip` / `filter` / `map`: the `Iterable[T]` slot refuses a readonly argument.** [`readonly-container-arg-refused-at-iterable-slot`] `def f(cells: readonly[list[Cell]]) -> int32: for i, c in enumerate(cells): ...` -> *Cannot pass readonly[list[Cell]] as mutable Iterable[Cell] in argument 'iterable'*; `reversed(cells)` (a `Sequence[T]` slot) is accepted, and an INFERRED-const `list[Cell]` parameter iterates through every combinator (the element comes back `const Cell&`, `tests/cases/builtins/combinator_elem_off_source`). The stubs are `@readonly` and lend the element in the form the source has it, so the readonly argument is fine; what is missing is the rule that a readonly argument at an iterator-returning stub's `Iterable[T]` slot makes the RESULT's element readonly (the loop var binds `const`), the same projection a `Span[readonly[T]]` argument already gets. Found 2026-09-22.
- **[HIGH small] (ill-formed C++, toolchain-caught; everyday shape) A COMPREHENSION that mutates through its loop variable over a PARAMETER keeps the parameter const, and the build fails.** [`comprehension-loop-var-mutation-not-propagated`] `def f(ns: list[Cell]) -> list[int32]: return [n.bump(1) for n in ns]` renders `const std::vector<Cell>& ns` and dies with *passing 'const Cell' as 'this' argument discards qualifiers*; the same with a combinator source (`[n.bump(1) for n in filter(pos, ns)]`, `[n.bump(x) for n, x in zip(ns, xs)]`). The `for` statement's twin demotes `ns` (a loop var carries `loop_var_iterable` / the ITER loan, and a write through it climbs to the source), but the comprehension route (`tpyc/sema/expressions.py`, `_enter_comp_scope`) installs no source provenance for its loop variable at all, so nothing there climbs -- over a local or a field the write compiles because those are never const. Fix shape: the comprehension's loop variable registers the same iterable provenance the for-statement registers (`_register_iter_loan` / `_register_iter_provenance_loan` in `tpyc/sema/statements.py`), so the mutation climb is one rule for both routes. Pre-existing and untracked before 2026-09-22 (found by the review of the combinator element-form unit; the comprehension sections of `tests/cases/builtins/combinator_elem_off_source` iterate locals and fields for this reason).
- **[MED small] (rejects valid, located) A generator declared `Iterator[Own[T]]` cannot be passed to a lazy combinator: `enumerate(make(3))` -> *No matching overload for enumerate(Iterator[Own[Cell]])*.** [`own-yield-generator-refused-at-iterable-slot`] The `Iterable[T]` slot does not match an `Iterator[Own[Cell]]` argument (the `Own` marker on the yield does not unify with `T`), while the compiler's own diagnostic steers a generator that yields fresh records INTO that spelling (*Cannot yield local or temporary as reference ... Declare the generator 'Iterator[Own[Cell]]'*), so a fresh-value generator cannot be enumerated or zipped at all. The runtime side is ready (a fresh step is owned by the combinator, `runtime/cpp/tests/test_combinator_elem_form.cpp`'s `Maker` legs); what is missing is the overload match, `Own[T]` unifying with the slot's `T` as the element that is then consumed. Found 2026-09-22.
- **[MED small] (hidden allocation, everyday shape) A `str` element steps through `enumerate` / `zip` / `reversed` as an owning `std::string` copy per element, where the plain `for` lends `const std::string&`.** [`combinator-str-element-copied-per-step`] `for i, s in enumerate(names)` over `list[str]` yields `std::tuple<int32_t, std::string>` (`detail::range_elem` carries every VALUE type by value, and `str` is one), so each step heap-copies the string to bind a `std::string_view` loop variable; `zip` and `reversed` (through `result_step_t`) do the same. The element-form rule is the natural place to carry a lent `str` as its view: a lent `std::string&` member could be handed on as `std::string_view` (the parameter form of `str`) with no copy. Pinned as the CURRENT form by a `static_assert` in `runtime/cpp/tests/test_combinator_elem_form.cpp` (section 5), which changes with this entry. Pre-existing (`val_or_ref_t<std::string>` copied too); found 2026-09-22.
- **[MED small] (rejects valid, located) `enumerate` over a `str` is a THIR reject (`stmt.for_each:iter.call.plain`).** [`enumerate-over-str-reject`] `for i, ch in enumerate(s)` with `s: str` stops at lowering, while `reversed(s)` and a plain `for ch in s` route; `zip(s, t)` over two strings is the same. The runtime side steps a `char` per element (`range_elem` over a `std::string_view` / `std::string`). Found 2026-09-22 while probing the combinator element forms.
- **[MED small] (no TPy diagnostic, raw C++ spew) `filter(None, xs)` over a list of RECORDS fails inside `to_bool` with a static-assert cascade.** [`filter-none-records-no-diagnostic`] `filter(None, cells)` with `cells: list[Cell]` renders `builtin_filter_truthy(cells)`, whose predicate calls `to_bool` on the record, and the runtime static-asserts with no located TPy diagnostic; CPython treats a record instance as truthy. `docs/LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md` calls `filter(None, ...)` a limitation, but the limitation surfaces as toolchain spew rather than a reject at the call. Found 2026-09-22.
- **[MED small] (ill-formed C++, toolchain-caught) A suspending `for` over a CONDITIONAL of two list params whose body mutates through the loop var does not compile: the params stay captured `const`.** [`frame-ternary-params-mutation-not-propagated`] `def g(xs: list[Cell], ys: list[Cell], flag: bool) -> Iterator[int32]: for c in (xs if flag else ys): c.v += 10; yield c.v` captures both params as `const std::vector<Cell>&`, so the loop var deduces `const Cell*` (its field is spelled off the source, `::tpy::begin_elem_t<decltype((flag ? xs : ys))>`) and the write is ill-formed. Cause: the for-head's loan registration (`_register_iter_loan` / `_register_iter_provenance_loan` in `tpyc/sema/statements.py`) files `loop_var_iterable` for a name, a subscript, a field or a call, and nothing for a conditional, so the write through the loop var climbs to no source; the shared provenance walker `lend_roots` (`tpyc/sema/scope_tracker.py`) does see both arms, and routing the for-head's non-lvalue sources through it is the fix shape (the call-edge side already does, since 2026-09-22). Narrowed 2026-09-22 from the const-spelling entry this replaced, which the source-typed fields closed.

Before the join the same program failed in the other loop (a mutable pointer seeded from a const_iterator), so the shape never compiled; what is missing is a located diagnostic -- sema's `mark_frame_const` already knows the binding is const from the first loop and could refuse the write there, or the two loops could take two fields. - **[MED small] (ill-formed C++, toolchain-caught) A loop variable bound by TWO `iter_next` loops takes one loop's source-form spelling for both.** [`frame-shared-loop-var-source-form-last-wins`] `for c in it_a: yield c.v` then `for c in it_b: yield c.v` over two user iterables in one frame declares `::tpy::frame_slot<::tpy::for_elem_next_t<__for_src_1_t>> c;` (the second loop's) and the first loop's advance writes through it; where the two sources lend differently (one hands back a reference, one a fresh value) the first loop's bind is ill-formed. `source_form_fields` in `_frame_layout` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/gen_async.py`) is last-wins, where the pointer-form payloads of the same layout are joined (`const_join_t`). Fix shape: join the two spellings the same way (a `frame_slot` over the common form), or give each loop its own field. Pre-existing on master (the same last-wins), surfaced by the tail review of the frame for-source unit, 2026-09-22.
- **[MED small] (rejects valid, located) A tuple-typed unpack TARGET over an iterator source in a frame is refused.** [`frame-unpack-tuple-target-local-storage`] `for i, p in enumerate(zip(xs, ys)): yield i + p[0] + p[1]` in a generator stops with `res.local_storage`: `p` is a `tuple[int32, int32]` bound from the step result's member, and the frame has no field form for a tuple member handed out of a step result (the value-tuple local arms admit a bind from a name or a call, not from an unpack). The flat twin `for i, (a, b) in ...` is not Python-legal at a `for` head in TPy's parser either way; `for a, b in zip(xs, ys)` and `for i, v in enumerate(reversed(xs))` compile. Surfaced by the tail review of the frame for-source unit, 2026-09-22.
- **[MED small] (ill-formed C++, toolchain-caught) A tuple-unpack `for` over `zip` of a list with `T | None` record elements fails the C++ build in an ORDINARY function.** [`zip-unpack-optional-record-element`] `for p, k in zip(a, b): out.append(p.v if p is not None else -1)` at `a: list[N | None]` -> `cannot convert 'std::optional<N>' to 'N*' in initialization`: the unpack target is spelled as the pointer-repr Optional (`N*`) but bound straight from the combinator's tuple member, which is the STORAGE optional. No genexpr and no frame involved. Found by the closing parity review 2026-09-20 (`/tmp/agents/review_gx2_parity/a12b_plainzip.py`); pre-existing.
- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A generator call bound to a local INSIDE a block is rejected.** [`generator-bound-inside-block-rejects`] `if c: g = relay(xs)` then `for v in g: print(v)` inside the same `if` -> `(expr.call:call.callee_kind)`, where the same two lines at function level compile. No genexpr is involved (`relay` is a plain `def` generator over a list). Found 2026-09-20 while checking the retained-genexpr rule against an `if`/`else` probe; not investigated further.
- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A NESTED generator expression as a comprehension or genexpr SOURCE rejects on both forms.** [`genexpr-nested-source`] `any(x > 1 for x in (y * 2 for y in xs))` -> `(expr.genexpr)`; `[x for x in (y * 2 for y in xs)]` -> `(expr.list_comp)`. The shared source classifier (`_source_route`, `tpyc/thir/lower/comprehensions.py`) has no arm for a `TpyGeneratorExpression` iterable; sema accepts both. Fix shape: an owned-rvalue arm like the generator-call one -- the inner genexpr's frame is a one-pass `next_iter_mixin` object, so the outer comp's `auto __obj_N = <inner>` capture drives it like a combinator, and the outer genexpr's frame builds it in place as its source. Workaround: materialize the inner one (`list(...)`) or fuse the two heads. Surfaced by the genexpr rvalue-source unification (`tests/cases/iterators/genexpr_rvalue_sources`).
- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) `for v in d.values(): t += v` at `d: readonly[dict[int32, int32]]` is a sema error: "Augmented assignment value must be a numeric type, got readonly[int32]".** [`readonly-value-element-leak`] The dict view stubs spell their value as `auto_readonly[V]`, so a readonly receiver types the element `readonly[int32]` -- but a VALUE element is copied into the loop var, and the readonly marker means nothing on a copy; sema's numeric checks do not peel it. The THIR lowering peels it for the loop-var binding and the comprehension / genexpr result slots (`_peel_value_readonly`, `tpyc/thir/lower/comprehensions.py`), so `sum(v for v in d.values())` and `[v for v in d.values()]` compile at a readonly receiver; only sema's own operator checks still see the marker. Fix shape: strip `readonly` off value-typed elements where the loop var / comp var is typed (`_resolve_comp_iterable` and the for-statement's element typing), or make `auto_readonly[V]` resolve to plain `V` for a value `V`. Either sema-side fix DELETES the three lowering peels (the `_peel_value_readonly` call sites in `_source_route`, the genexpr unpack head and the comprehension unpack head), which exist only because sema hands the marker down. Probe `/tmp/agents/gx/ro_for.py`.
- **[MED small] (ill-formed C++, toolchain-caught) A comprehension unpack head over a dict `items()` view (or any proxy-tuple combinator) with an all-scalar tuple binds `auto& __tup_N = *__beg_N;` to a PRVALUE.** [`comp-unpack-prvalue-tuple`] `[k + v for k, v in d.items()]` at `dict[int32, int32]` fails the C++ build with `cannot bind non-const lvalue reference of type 'std::tuple<const int&, const int&>&' to an rvalue` -- the items iterator's `reference` is a proxy tuple returned by value (`ordered_map::tuple_items_iterator_impl`), and sema's `const_loop_var` (`worth_const_ref`, `tpyc/sema/expressions.py`) is False for a value tuple that is not expensive to copy, so the emit picks `auto&` instead of the `const auto&` that binds a prvalue (`dict_comp_unpack` passes only because its str value makes the tuple worth a const ref). (A genexpr's frame has no such bind: its unpack holder points at the step result in the frame's own slot.) Fix shape: bind the unpack tuple `auto&&` in `_emit_comprehension` too (spelling-only churn on the non-const comp snapshots). Probe `/tmp/agents/gx/items_comp.py`. Surfaced by the genexpr rvalue-source unification.
- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, masked) A generator expression whose SOURCE CALL needs a hoisted argument temp rejects, where the comprehension over the same call compiles.** [`genexpr-source-needs-arg-temp`] `sum(v for v in make(Box(8)))` with `def make(b: Box[int32]) -> Own[list[int32]]` -> `(expr.genexpr)` (the landmark face; the inner reason is the no-temps arg gate), while `[v for v in make(Box(8))]` compiles and hoists `Box<int32_t> __tmp_1 = Box<int32_t>(8);` ahead of its statement -- the `@nocopy` ctor temp a by-reference param needs. `_lower_genexpr_frame` lowers its source with no temp right (`tpyc/thir/lower/comprehensions.py`), while the comprehension route threads `allow_temps=True` (its source renders at statement level; `docs/COMPREHENSION_DESIGN.md` documents the asymmetry). An owned source renders inside the in-place factory lambda, which captures by reference, so a temp flushed ahead of the enclosing statement is reachable from it wherever the position has a flush point. A generic factory's scalar literal arg (`make(8, 3)` at `n: T`) hoists no temp and works on both forms. Fix shape: thread the enclosing position's temp right into the source lowering, so both forms admit the same arg shapes. Workaround: bind the argument to a local first. Probe `/tmp/agents/review_genexpr_fix/arg_temp_box.py`. Found reviewing the genexpr rvalue-source unification 2026-09-13.
- **[MED small] (ill-formed C++, toolchain-caught; would be a CPython divergence if it built) Binding a started generator to a second name COPIES its frame.** [`generator-rebind-copies-frame`] `t = gen(3)` then `t2 = t`, then `for v in t2:` fails the C++ build with `use of deleted function '__gen_gen::__gen_gen(const __gen_gen&)'` -- the assignment renders a copy of the frame struct, whose `frame_slot` / `frame_loop_slot` members delete the copy ctor (identically on master). In CPython the two names are the SAME generator: advancing `t2` advances `t`, and iterating one after the other yields nothing the second time. So the copy the emit asks for is not just non-copyable, it is the wrong semantics; a frame with no slot member would compile and silently diverge. No diagnostic names the construct. Fix shape: a generator local rebind is a MOVE (the source is dead afterwards, matching the `Own[Iterator]` param rule) or a reject naming the construct -- not a copy. Found checking probe fallout from /tpy-review of the generator-frame perf branch 2026-09-17; probe `/tmp/agents/p3b.py`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (ill-formed C++, toolchain-caught) A lazy combinator that OWNS a user-iterable temporary with a separate iterator cannot be moved into another owning consumer.** [`separate-iter-temp-no-flush-slot`] `zip(Noisy(2), xs)` with `def __iter__(self) -> Own[Cur]`: where the position has a statement-level slot and the temporary is a constructor or free-function call, tpyc binds it to a local and the combinator BORROWS it (`argtemp.separate_iter_source`), staying movable. Everywhere else -- a nested call argument, a member init, a genexpr's source, module level, an `and`/`or` operand, a method / static-factory / field-of-temporary source -- the combinator owns the record in place and is PINNED (`detail::owned_iter_source`, `runtime/cpp/include/tpy/itertools.hpp`: its `__iter__` is user code that runs at the call and the iterator may point into the record), exactly the pre-2026-09-18 behaviour. A pinned combinator handed to another OWNING consumer in such a position (`print(list(enumerate(zip(h.make(), xs))))`) fails the C++ build with a deleted move ctor, as every owning combinator nested in another did before they became movable; the GENEXPR face (`enumerate(a * b for a, b in zip(Noisy(2), xs))` -- a genexpr's source never has a slot, so its combinator is always pinned) is a located reject instead, `genexpr.pinned_into_owning`, pinned by `tests/cases/iterators/error_genexpr_pinned_into_owning`. Rare on three axes; zero occurrences in the test corpus and the stdlib. Workaround: bind the object first (`n = h.make()`). Closes when "Producers are movable only while unstarted" (TODO.md) gives the pinned kind a movable form.
- **[LOW small] (silent CPython divergence) A resumable frame's `for` over a SELF-ITERATOR never calls the user's `__iter__`, and neither does a container built from one.** [`frame-for-skips-self-iterator-iter`] `resumable_iter_init` (`runtime/cpp/include/tpy/generator.hpp`) emplaces an iterator only for a non-self source, and a self-iterator (`def __iter__(self): return self`) is driven through `__next__` directly, so a side effect in its `__iter__` disappears inside a generator or `async def` body; `list(iter(Quiet(2)))` constructs the list off the returned iterator's begin/end the same way, where CPython's `list()` calls `iter()` on it once more. An ordinary function's loop and the lazy combinators run it. Found reviewing the owning-combinator move 2026-09-18, which fixed the same skip in the combinators.
- **[MED small] (compiler crash) A MODULE-LEVEL `for a, b in zip(xs, ys):` dies with `Internal error: list index out of range`.** [`module-level-zip-unpack-ice`] Plain lists, no temporaries; the same loop inside a function compiles. Found reviewing the owning-combinator move 2026-09-18; reproduces at the branch point.
- **[LOW small] (silent CPython divergence, pre-existing) An `__iter__` that mutation inference marks `@readonly` hands its iterator back as a CONST reference, so a combinator iterates a copy.** [`readonly-iter-result-iterated-as-copy`] `class Wrap: def __iter__(self) -> Cur: return SHARED` (a module-level `Cur`): the method never mutates `self`, is inferred readonly, and renders `const Cur& __iter__() const`; nothing can pull through a const reference, so the combinators copy it (`detail::iter_cursor` / `iter_member_t`, `runtime/cpp/include/tpy/itertools.hpp`) and `zip(Wrap(), xs)` leaves `SHARED.i` at 0 where CPython reads the advanced count. - **[LOW small] (diagnostic quality) An arg temp with no statement-level slot rejects as `protocol arg-temp outside a flush position`, internal wording in a user-facing error.** [`argtemp-no-flush-slot-wording`] Shared by every `argtemp.*` render arm in `tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py`; the module-level and genexpr-source positions are where users meet it.
- **[HIGH small] (ill-formed C++, toolchain-caught) A tuple-unpack `for` target rebound by a plain assignment AFTER the loop is assigned inside the loop with no declaration.** [`loop-unpack-target-rebound-after-loop`] `for i, v in enumerate(xs): print(i, v)` followed by `i = 0` fails the C++ build (`'i' was not declared in this scope` at the loop's `i = std::get<0>(__tup_N);`): the later assignment makes `i` a function-level rebind, so the loop stops declaring it per iteration, and nothing declares it ahead of the loop. Everyday shape -- an index variable reused as a counter (`i = 0; while i < n:`). A SINGLE loop variable (`for i in xs: ...; i = 0`) and a second `for i, v in ...` over the same names both compile; so does the same shape in a generator body whose loop does not suspend, where the name is a frame member (verified 2026-09-20). Probes `/tmp/agents/gx/fx/u1.py` (fails), `u2.py`, `u4.py` (compile). Found writing `tests/cases/builtins/combinator_owned_source_moves` 2026-09-18.
- **[MED small] (silent CPython divergence, pre-existing) A subclass that declares `__next__` gets a synthesized `__iter__` that hides its base's user-written one.** [`synthesized-iter-shadows-base-iter`] `tpyc/codegen_cpp/records.py` emits `auto& __iter__() { return *this; }` for a record declaring `__next__`, keyed on the record's OWN methods only, so `class Sub(Base)` overriding `__next__` while inheriting a `Base.__iter__` with a side effect never runs it -- in a plain `for` and in every combinator (CPython prints the base's trace; TPy prints nothing). - **[LOW small] (diagnostic hygiene) The internal `PendingList` spelling leaks into a protocol-conformance error.** [`pendinglist-in-conformance-diag`] `def each(xs: Iterable[list[int32]])` fed a bare `[[1], [2]]` errors `Type PendingList[PendingList[IntLiteral(1), 1]#0, 2]#2 does not conform to protocol Iterable[list[int32]] in argument 'xs'` -- `PendingList`, `IntLiteral` and the `#N` id are compiler internals a user cannot write, which `docs/PITFALLS.md#no-internal-names-in-diagnostics` forbids in a user-facing message. - **[LOW small] (rejects-valid + diagnostic hygiene) A SLICE of an unannotated list local at a `Span[T]` param is rejected, and the message spells the internal `IntLiteral`.** [`intliteral-in-span-slice-arg-diag`] `xs = [1, 2, 3]; take(xs[0:2])` against `def take(s: Span[int32])` errors `Type mismatch in argument 's': expected Span[int32], got Span[IntLiteral(1)]` -- the slice's span is built off the literal's un-widened element type, so the arg check compares `Span[IntLiteral(1)]` against `Span[int32]`. Two defects at once: the code is valid (the annotated `xs: list[int32] = [1, 2, 3]` gets past sema, then rejects at codegen's `call.arg_shape.span`, which is the separate slice-source gate), and `IntLiteral(1)` is a spelling no user can write, which `docs/PITFALLS.md#no-internal-names-in-diagnostics` forbids in a user-facing message. Passing the same local WHOLE (`take(xs)`) compiles, so only the slice path skips the element widening. Distinct from `BUGS.md#pendinglist-in-conformance-diag` and the pending-container diagnostic entry further down: no `PendingList` survives here -- the container resolved and only its ELEMENT stayed literal -- so a `PendingList`-only rendering helper would not touch it; the literal-element leak is shared with the repeat-literal entry below (`[0.0] * n`).
